question: Which parts of Elephants by the Lake are doing best and which parts are struggling? Give our field team a short priority map or ranked list of places to inspect next.
answer:
I'll look through the workspace for Elephants by the Lake data and any performance or status metrics so we can rank what to inspect next.Workspace looks empty — checking transcripts and available data sources next.Found a Tamil Nadu project by that name — digging into their site zones and any published monitoring data.Pulling the EBTL site and Ananas project updates for zone-level status.Found the site map and newsletter drive — pulling those plus the restoration page for zone-level detail.Coordinates are in — next I'll pull zone-level greening from satellite data and dig through the newsletters/forum for ground reports.Downloading the EBTL newsletters and faunal survey — those should have the zone-level performance detail.Newsletters name a clear north–south attention gap — reading the June 2023 and faunal survey next, then checking greening from satellite.Inspecting the newsletter maps that mark attended vs untreated areas, and sampling satellite greening across the site.Computing zone-level NDVI from Sentinel-2 to back the newsletter findings with satellite evidence.CRS mismatch was the issue — recomputing NDVI with proper UTM projection.**Verdict:** The nursery and northern waterworks are the strongest parts of EBTL; the **southern parcels**, **mango orchards (especially wetland-sited ones)**, and **drought-stressed 2023 plantings** are the main places to inspect next.

---

### Field priority map (inspect in this order)

| Rank | Place (site map labels) | Status | Why inspect next |
|------|-------------------------|--------|------------------|
| **1** | **Southern restoration & wild zones** (toward Veppanapilly RF) | Under-attended until mid-2024; now the stated push | July 2024 newsletter: south “has received little attention till now”; plan was cluster planting + leave regeneration gaps |
| **2** | **Mango orchard blocks (~20 acres)** — especially trees in **potential wetlands** | Struggling / mismatche | Remove failing mangoes; check native interplants; wetlands are wrong microhabitat for mango |
| **3** | **Already-treated “green circle” plots** (earthworks + 2023 plantings near catchments) | Recovering after failed monsoon | ~6,000+ natives planted; needed emergency irrigation; start survival M&E here first |
| **4** | **Northern wetland, percolation ponds, northernmost pond + swales** | Doing relatively well | Core water system; check siltation, bund/swale damage, wildlife water rings after monsoon |
| **5** | **Wild-zone irrigation lines / forest edge** | Damage + conflict pressure | May 2024 elephant crushed pipes; deer/boar at ponds; HEC risk nearby |
| **6** | **Vegetable / food-garden beds** | Paused under drought | Left idle to spare water for nursery; check wildlife browse and whether beds need rebuild |
| **7** | **Native nursery** | Best-performing | 110 spp / ~15k capacity; sapling giveaways — routine check only |

**Doing best (monitor, don’t divert scarce labour):** nursery; northern water catchments/ponds; planted plots that put out new shoots after June 2024 rains.  
**Struggling / high risk:** southern untreated land (management gap); wetland mangoes; drought-hit plantings without a survival census; elephant-damaged infrastructure on the wild edge.

---

### Method (so you can check it)

**Sources**
1. Official zone map: [ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/) (`/static/images/ebtl-map-new.png`) — wetland, percolation ponds, Panchayat lake, nursery/food garden, learning/living, restoration & wild zones, Veppanapilly RF.
2. Newsletters (Google Drive folder linked from the site): [June 2023](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1t1_X4f1PjG2YhZtM8Qio8E8cmaKkNLk-/view), [Oct 2023](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PcpKa3bYnJxw0s78qdwWhn_WDAW-IvqE/view), [Feb/Mar 2024](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1f1R1rHA_rjCHDDqB4nHTtrXVWC-Le2CF/view), [July 2024](https://drive.google.com/file/d/122I9j4fVdXYpfqMCGb2n4gNFTtRsXEwb/view).
3. Location: Plus Code **P5MM+H9**, Budhimutlu (~12.7339°N, 78.1834°E).
4. Sentinel-2 L2A NDVI (Microsoft Planetary Computer), ~90×90 m windows around zone centroids, PB≥4 offset applied.

**Key ground facts used**
- Green circles on the July 2024 map = waterworks + invasive clearing + planting already done.
- South flagged as next work area (July 2024).
- 2023 NE monsoon largely failed → hills brown, saplings irrigated from open well; veg beds paused; farm wildlife raids up.
- Mango monoculture on ~20 acres; some in wetlands; remove struggling trees + interplant natives.
- Nursery healthy enough to donate saplings.

**Satellite cross-check (NDVI mean)**

| Zone sample | Dry 2024-03-23 | Dry 2025-04-12 | Post-mono 2025-12-08 |
|-------------|----------------|----------------|----------------------|
| N wetland / percolation | 0.23 | 0.37 | 0.66 |
| N lake edge | 0.22 | 0.30 | 0.65 |
| Mid nursery / food garden | 0.24 | 0.44 | 0.66 |
| Mid mango (est.) | 0.30 | 0.45 | 0.66 |
| Mid learning/living | 0.32 | 0.45 | 0.40 |
| S restoration/wild | 0.34 | 0.57 | 0.77 |
| S far south / reserve edge | 0.33 | 0.56 | 0.78 |
| Ref: Veppanapilly forest | 0.31 | 0.51 | 0.77 |

**How to read this with the newsletters:** South is greenest (forest-edge / reserve influence), so high NDVI ≠ “job done”—it still ranks **#1 for inspection** because management attention lagged. North is driest in the dry season but recovers strongly after rain (wetland phenology + waterworks). Mid campus built area stays low NDVI by design. Year-on-year dry NDVI rose across zones after the bad 2023 monsoon (+0.08 to +0.23).

**Caveats:** Zone points are approximate centroids from the public map + Maps pin, not surveyed plot polygons. NDVI does not separate planted natives from mango, weeds, or forest spillover. No public plot-level survival rates yet (M&E was only starting as of July 2024).The first satellite NDVI job hung and was stopped; a cleaner re-run finished successfully and those numbers are already in the priority map above. No change to the inspection ranking.

Synthesis:
Monitoring elephants near lakes typically involves non-invasive field techniques focused on population estimation, demographic data collection, and habitat use [1][2][3]. Common methods include:

Direct observations: Researchers conduct herd counts and record group composition, age, sex, and individual IDs [1][4]. To avoid double-counting, protocols often specify recording only groups that arrive at the lake after researchers are present [1][5].

Dung counts: Researchers use line transects or quadrants to count dung piles to estimate relative abundance and density [2][4][3]. Samples are also analyzed to assess diet, crop consumption, and potential human-elephant conflict [1][6][5].

Infrastructure and support: Monitoring often utilizes camera traps to detect elusive individuals [7][6], GPS to track movements [1], and community-based models to stabilize populations in fragmented landscapes [8]. 

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) is a forest restoration and research project based in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, that integrates field monitoring, ecological baseline creation, and molecular genetics to support biodiversity conservation in the Eastern Ghats [9][10].

Synthesis:
Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) is a community-driven forest restoration project located at the base of the Krishnagiri hills in Tamil Nadu [1][2]. Supported by the Rainmatter Foundation and managed by the team at Ananas, the project focuses on regenerating approximately 70 acres of land using permaculture principles to restore native dry deciduous forest flora [3][2][4]. EBTL also operates an in-house research initiative, the Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies, to study biodiversity and support ecological conservation [1][5][6]. The site functions as a residential learning center for nature-based education and rural livelihoods [7][8].

success.markdown:
Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) - A forest restoration project in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu

Over decades, the dry deciduous forests of our country have been stripped and exploited for commercial use. As native forests receded to only higher elevations of hills, creatures of the forests have also lost their footing in the valley. EBTL lies in one of those valleys. In the foothills of a degraded forest.

These 70 acres now 'belong' to us. How wonderful would it be if the other creatures also echoed the same thought? Our goal is to help the forest regain its rich biodiversity.

The year we began work, a few elephants came to the land, something that had never happened in the last many decades. We decided to call this project.

# Elephants By The Lake!

# The map of EBTL

Once you step into the hills around EBTL there are remnants of a once thriving forest; bird calls, fresh bear tracks, the jumping away of a troupe of langurs, trees in bloom or seed, spiders waiting for a catch, the scuffling across of a monitor lizard, a bird of prey gliding above.

Unfortunately this biodiverse ecosystem of the Eastern Ghats has been almost eradicated in terms of its area, but for a few hilly pockets where the tough terrain has made it too difficult for people to interfere.

Hopefully in time, the land will begin a cycle of regeneration where at a point, this space can become a safe corner for some of the rarer and threatened flora of the Eastern Ghats to flourish and wildlife can reinhabit the land.

# What happens at EBTL

#### Forest restoration

EBTL, primarily is focused on the native flora of the dry decidious forests of the South Deccan plateau.

#### Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies

We have established a dedicated in-house field research initiative at our campus in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, to address critical gaps in knowledge about Eastern Ghats biodiversity, ecology, and conservation priorities.

#### Organic farming

A small percentage of land we own is allotted for farming where we grow paddy, pulses, millets and vegetables.

#### Farmer's Collective

We work very closely with the nearby village of Chinnathamandrapalli. The villagers play a vital role in all the work we undertake. We have enabled a collective of women working towards value added products. They also manage our farm lands and campus.

# Farmer's Collective

We promote land stewardship and sustainable farming by employing the local community and supporting a farmers collective to create value-added products. Our goal is to provide eco-friendly job opportunities to counter urban migration among the younger generation.

Elephants By The Lake!

The map of EBTL

Unfortunately this biodiverse ecosystem of the Eastern Ghats has been almost eradicated in terms of its area, but for a few hilly pockets where the tough terrain has made it too difficult for people to interfere.

Hopefully in time, the land will begin a cycle of regeneration where at a point, this space can become a safe corner for some of the rarer and threatened flora of the Eastern Ghats to flourish and wildlife can reinhabit the land.

A small percentage of land we own is allotted for farming where we grow paddy, pulses, millets and vegetables.

We promote land stewardship and sustainable farming by employing the local community and supporting a farmers collective to create value-added products. Our goal is to provide eco-friendly job opportunities to counter urban migration among the younger generation.

restoration.html:

We have raised more than a 130 species of native flora and 15,000 saplings. Once saplings are of a certain age they are planted in the land during the monsoon months. Once planted and mulched we rely mostly on the rains to take care that the saplings don't dry out.

restoration.html:

    EBTL is designed and managed by a ground team that lives on site with the support of Rainmatter foundation.  Our primary focus in the initial three years were developing a native tree nursery and also understanding the land with respect to water flows during monsoons. We have also intervened with mix of strategies like active tree planting, removal of invasives and natural regeneration of land. For this we have also collaborated with a few practitioners whose names are mentioned below.

    about.html:

    Post realising the lack of interest in my engineering degree, I spent many years travelling and volunteering in animal shelters and wildlife rescue centres. The diversity in the natural world has always fascinated me, how should one comprehend the many ways in which the same world is perceived by different life forms? And how as a species we find our position in this intricate web of beings. Living and working in EBTL gives me a unique opportunity to be a student of the natural world and pursue my different passions- art, farming, wildlife, forests and many more interests yet to be discovered.

    ` about.html:

    For a few years now have been working on restoration in degraded land areas. Have been documenting flora, understanding past human landscape interactions, raising native plant nurseries and doing planting.

    about.html:

    This has been in Eastern Ghats hill ranges of Krishnagiri and more recently in the aslo in the Nilgiris in abandoned coffee estates. At EBTL, I lead the seed collection work and established the nursery. I also took care of the planting work and managing the restoration site. Currently I focus on carrying out Monitoring and evaluation of restored sites at EBTL.

    ` about.html:

    The network of interconnectedness within nature has always surprised me. Currently I manage the native flora nursery in EBTL and also work the citizen science programmes.     EBTL is designed and managed by a ground team that lives on site with the support of Rainmatter foundation.  Our primary focus in the initial three years were developing a native tree nursery and also understanding the land with respect to water flows during monsoons. We have also intervened with mix of strategies like active tree planting, removal of invasives and natural regeneration of land. For this we have also collaborated with a few practitioners whose names are mentioned below.

    about.html:

    Post realising the lack of interest in my engineering degree, I spent many years travelling and volunteering in animal shelters and wildlife rescue centres. The diversity in the natural world has always fascinated me, how should one comprehend the many ways in which the same world is perceived by different life forms? And how as a species we find our position in this intricate web of beings. Living and working in EBTL gives me a unique opportunity to be a student of the natural world and pursue my different passions- art, farming, wildlife, forests and many more interests yet to be discovered.

    ` about.html:

    For a few years now have been working on restoration in degraded land areas. Have been documenting flora, understanding past human landscape interactions, raising native plant nurseries and doing planting.

    about.html:

    This has been in Eastern Ghats hill ranges of Krishnagiri and more recently in the aslo in the Nilgiris in abandoned coffee estates. At EBTL, I lead the seed collection work and established the nursery. I also took care of the planting work and managing the restoration site. Currently I focus on carrying out Monitoring and evaluation of restored sites at EBTL.

    ` about.html:

    The network of interconnectedness within nature has always surprised me. In 2021, I did a 3 month horticulture course in Auroville botanical gardens after which I volunteered with The Forestway in Thiruvanamalai. I have spent a lot of time exploring the dry deciduous forests of the south Deccan plateau, and being a part of the EBTL on ground team enables me to explore even further. Currently I manage the native flora nursery in EBTL and also work the citizen science programmes. I look forward to going more into the forests around, teaching myself about the life in them and in the process contribute to the restoration work on ground.

    ` about.html: title: "Wildlife photographer", about.html:

    I am a professional wildlife photographer, photography mentor and naturalist. After an engineering degree and an MBA, I worked in the corporate world briefly before I realised my passion for wildlife and photography. I have travelled to wildlife habitats around the world, including rainforests, polar regions, high altitude Himalayas, deserts and islands. I build photography narratives that weave in creative perspectives along with natural history and conservation principles. I have published my stories in diverse print and digital magazines such as National Geographic Traveller, Sanctuary Asia, Saevus, Lonely Planet India, Round Glass Sustain, Nature inFocus and JLR Explore.

    about.html:

    I mentors enthusiastic photographers on wildlife photography tours across the world.As a naturalist, I have trained and certified naturalists across Karnataka in association with Jungle Lodges and Resorts and Karnataka Eco-tourism Development Board. I was also part of a team that described 2 new species of geckos from the dry regions of Karnataka.

    about.html:

    At EBTL, I am documenting and photographing wildlife across the campus and surrounding areas to gain a better understanding of the wildlife in the region and the impact of restoration initiatives in enhancing their habitat.

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) - A forest restoration project in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu

# Restoration project

We are trying to restore the land to a good ecological health using the little pockets of healthy forests as a reference in knowing what kind of an ecosystem is possible here.

We are focusing primarily in active restoration in the form of collecting seeds from the forest remnants of this region as well as from nearby reserve forests in the ecoregion to raise a nursery and carry out planting.

We have raised more than a 130 species of native flora and 15,000 saplings. Once saplings are of a certain age they are planted in the land during the monsoon months. Once planted and mulched we rely mostly on the rains to take care that the saplings don't dry out.

Natural regeneration is also a process that takes place in the land as we are sufficiently close to the forest. High wildlife activity helps in ensuring that some seeds get dispersed in the land.

# Our vision

To restore ecological balance by nurturing native flora and enriching the biodiversity on the land. Using healthy forest pockets as our inspiration, we’re developing a sustainable ecosystem that can thrive with minimal intervention.

#### Seed Collection and Nursery

Using seeds sourced from local forest remnants and nearby reserve forests, we cultivate over 100 species of native flora and currently have around 15,000 saplings. Each seedling is cared for in trays, pots, and bags until they reach planting maturity.

#### Planting Process

During the monsoon, mature saplings are transplanted and mulched on the land, relying mostly on natural rain for sustenance. We also see some natural regeneration due to high wildlife activity, as animals help disperse seeds.

# The Ecoregion

Our site is nestled in the unique Deccan Dry Deciduous Forest ecoregion, where deciduous and evergreen trees thrive alongside a wide range of shrubs and climbers. As we explore the secluded hills around the site, we uncover remnants of what once were lush forests, hinting at the ecological richness we aim to restore.

#### Flora Diversity

We encounter a diverse array of trees including Chloroxylon swietenia, Diospyros montana, Wrightia tinctoria, and Ficus tsjahela, which are native to this area. These species form a vital part of the dense canopy in less disturbed areas and are essential for ecological balance.

#### Fauna in the Region

The land is also a natural habitat for an impressive range of fauna including the Sloth Bear, Amur Falcon, Indian Rock Python, and Asian Elephant. The diversity of wildlife plays a critical role in sustaining this ecosystem.

# Volunteering at EBTL

Join us in our journey towards a greener, richer ecosystem. By nurturing these lands and reintroducing native species, we hope to restore the ecological balance that once thrived here.

Write to [email protected] to know more

Elephants by the Lake (EBTL) is a Rainmatter Foundation project focused on regenerating approximately 70 acres of land in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, using permaculture principles [1][2][3]. Ananas Permaculture was engaged to execute this restoration work [1][4]. While public project updates were shared during the initial stages of the partnership [1][4], there is no centralized report or newsletter specifically titled Ananas restoration update for 2023, 2024, or 2025. Synthesis:
Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) is a forest restoration project in Tamil Nadu, India, focused on regenerating native deciduous forests and enhancing biodiversity on 70 acres of degraded land [1][2]. The project manages a native forest nursery and plants saplings during the monsoon season [3]. While the organization conducts field research and monitors the landscape, its publicly available materials do not specifically document using NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) for survival rate tracking or invasive species management [1][4][3]. Scientific studies elsewhere use NDVI to monitor elephant-induced vegetation changes, but this is not identified as an EBTL methodology [5][6].

<content># Using piospheres to identify, assess and monitor gradients of elephant impact on thicket
...
Abstract Overpopulation in conservation areas with large populations of elephants reduces the diversity of the thicket vegetation of the Eastern Cape Province of South Africa. Monitoring species' specific impacts is a difficult task for reserves. This study investigates whether the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) can be used to evaluate the health of thicket in the Addo Elephant National Park successfully. To achieve this, different browsing intensities of elephants were used to establish a gradient of the full range of utilisation levels on thicket. These were obtained at different distances from the nearest available water sources for Mesic and Valley Thicket types. NDVI values were correlated to an elephant utilisation gradient, which was, in turn, directly related to distance from a water source. The lowest NDVI values (<0.2) were observed adjacent to watering holes where vegetation was completely degraded due to trampling by the daily congregation of animals. The highest NDVI values (>0.5 representing the densest stands of thicket vegetation) were obtained at distances exceeding 7 km from a water source where elephant densities were the lowest within the park. NDVI values could, therefore, be used to identify and monitor gradients of elephant impact on the integrity of thicket.

args.command:
cd /tmp/ebtl
# Fix june 2023 download from grove link
curl -sL "https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1t1_X4f1PjG2YhZtM8Qio8E8cmaKkNLk-" -o june2023b.pdf
file june2023b.pdf
# Extract text from PDFs
python3 <<'PY'
import subprocess, os
files = ['july2024.pdf','march2024.pdf','oct2023.pdf','faunal2024.pdf','june2023.pdf','june2023b.pdf']
for f in files:
    if not os.path.exists(f) or os.path.getsize(f)<1000:
        print(f'SKIP {f}'); continue
    out=f.replace('.pdf','.txt')
    # try pdftotext
    r=subprocess.run(['pdftotext','-layout',f,out],capture_output=True,text=True)
    if r.returncode!=0:
        print(f'pdftotext fail {f}: {r.stderr[:200]}')
        # try pypdf
        try:
            from pypdf import PdfReader
            reader=PdfReader(f)
            text='\n'.join((p.extract_text() or '') for p in reader.pages)
            open(out,'w').write(text)
            print(f'pypdf ok {f} pages={len(reader.pages)} chars={len(text)}')
        except Exception as e:
            print(f'fail {f}',e)
    else:
        print(f'ok {f} -> {out} size={os.path.getsize(out)}')
PY
ls -la *.txt 2>/dev/null

WHAT’S NEW AT



ELEPHANTS
BY THE LAKE
                June 2023
                                      During the dry summer months, with temperatures
                                     reaching around 35-40°C, our efforts at Elephants
                                     by the Lake had primarily focussed on planning and
                                     maintenance work, which involved sapling care in the
                                     nursery, desilting old earthworks and making compost
                                     for the upcoming planting season. A few volunteers from
                                     Zerodha joined us at the site over the past two months,
                                     and we plan to have more in the coming months.

                                     Come June, the anticipation of monsoon has ramped
                                     up activities we have been planning all summer. Our
                                     current priorities encompass shaping water systems,
                                     establishing and maintaining the nursery for plant
                                     propagation, generating biomass to restore land carbon
                                     and microbiomes, and other related activities.

                                     It is important to note that restoration work can be
                                     approached through multiple strategies and methods,
                                     and in this respect our focus has been on a deeper
                                     observation and understanding of ecological processes.
                                     While conventional methods of tree planting or “greening”
                                     focus on high resource use, our aim is to accelerate
                                     recovery in the way nature likes to recover, creating
                                     conditions favourable for soil, plants and water to nudge
                                     the complex system to ever higher orders of stability.

                                     In this monthly newsletter, we aim to provide insights into
                                     our thought process, explaining the rationale behind our
                                     chosen strategies and decision-making which are shaped
                                     by the land. We will also share our learning experiences
                                     as we continue to familiarise ourselves with the processes

Methodology

 Time-constrained Visual Encounter Surveys (VES) were
employed to evaluate the presence and abundance of the
targeted groups. This technique involves observers
conducting a visual search for a set period in a designated
area. VES is commonly utilized in biodiversity
assessments, population monitoring, and habitat quality
evaluations. Observers record all species seen and heard
during the survey, noting the number of individuals
observed. This data offers valuable insights into species
richness and relative abundance. The fixed observation
duration enables standardized data collection, facilitating
easier comparisons of results across various surveys and
locations.
 While VES is efficient, it may not detect all species
present, especially for cryptic groups such as reptiles and
amphibians that are secretive or have low visibility.
Therefore, thorough searches were conducted in various
potential hideouts for reptiles and amphibains. All species
were surveyed according to their activity patterns; for
instance, butterflies and odonates were counted during
their peak activity hours, between 10 AM and 4 PM, while
amphibians and reptiles were also surveyed during the
night between 07.30 and 09.30 pm.

Survey Dates
1. Ornithology – 5th to 7th Sept 2024
2. Herpetology – 5th to 7th Sept 2024
3. Lepidopterology – 5th to 7th Sept 2024
4. Odonatology – 10th to 13th Oct 2024
 Butterflies of EBTL
M. A. Yathumon

Methods
Butterflies were surveyed using transect walks to estimate
their relative abundance. Transects were along existing
roads and walkways, with four transects conducted daily,
each lasting 30 minutes, over three days from 5th to 7th
September, 2024. Surveys were carried out between 09:30
AM and 12:30 PM, recording all butterflies observed on
either side of the road, noting species and number of
individuals. A checklist of species was compiled using all
observations, both during and outside of the transect walks.

Results
A total of 54 species from 5 families were recorded during
the three-day survey. The family Nymphalidae had the
highest number of species recorded, followed by Pieridae,
Lycaenidae, Papilionidae, and Hesperiidae (Figure 1).

import json, urllib.request, urllib.parse
# Search recent Sentinel-2 L2A near EBTL
lat, lon = 12.7338909, 78.1833954
# bbox ~70 acres ~ 0.5km extent - use ~800m box
d = 0.006  # ~650m
bbox = [lon-d, lat-d, lon+d, lat+d]
# dry season (Mar-May) and wet season (Oct-Nov) comparisons
queries = [
    ('2025-10-01','2025-12-15','post-monsoon 2025'),
    ('2024-10-01','2024-12-15','post-monsoon 2024'),
    ('2024-03-01','2024-05-31','dry 2024'),
    ('2025-03-01','2025-05-31','dry 2025'),
]
base = 'https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1/search'
for start,end,label in queries:
    body = {
        "collections": ["sentinel-2-l2a"],
        "bbox": bbox,
        "datetime": f"{start}T00:00:00Z/{end}T23:59:59Z",
        "query": {"eo:cloud_cover": {"lt": 20}},
        "limit": 5,
        "sortby": [{"field": "eo:cloud_cover", "direction": "asc"}]
    }
    req = urllib.request.Request(base, data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={'Content-Type':'application/json'})
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as r:
            data = json.load(r)
        feats = data.get('features',[])
        print(f'\n=== {label} ({start}..{end}): {len(feats)} scenes ===')
        for f in feats[:3]:
            props=f['properties']
            print(props.get('datetime'), 'cloud', props.get('eo:cloud_cover'), f['id'])
    except Exception as e:
        print(label, 'ERR', e)

args.command:
python3 <<'PY'
import json, urllib.request, statistics, struct, math
from io import BytesIO

try:
    import numpy as np
    from PIL import Image
except ImportError:
    import subprocess
    subprocess.check_call(['pip','install','-q','numpy','pillow','rasterio','rioxarray','planetary-computer','pystac-client'])
    import numpy as np
    from PIL import Image

import planetary_computer as pc
from pystac_client import Client

catalog = Client.open("https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1")

# Zone centroids based on site map + Google Maps place ~12.7339, 78.1834
# Rough parcel orientation N-S along ~78.18
zones = {
    "N_wetland_percolation": (12.7365, 78.1830),
    "N_panchayat_lake_edge": (12.7355, 78.1815),
    "mid_nursery_food_garden": (12.7345, 78.1825),
    "mid_learning_living": (12.7340, 78.1840),
    "mid_mango_orchard_est": (12.7330, 78.1820),
    "S_restoration_wild": (12.7315, 78.1835),
    "S_far_south_toward_reserve": (12.7300, 78.1840),
    "ref_veppanapilly_forest": (12.7285, 78.1855),
}

scenes = [
    ("2025-12-08 dry-season-green", "S2C_MSIL2A_20251208T051221_R019_T43PHQ_20251208T081319"),
    ("2024-12-08 post-monsoon", "S2B_MSIL2A_20241208T051119_R019_T43PHQ_20241208T075639"),
    ("2024-03-23 drought-era", "S2B_MSIL2A_20240323T050649_R019_T43PHQ_20240323T101425"),
    ("2025-04-12 dry", "S2C_MSIL2A_20250412T050711_R019_T43PHQ_20250412T102015"),
]

# Use STAC item search by ID
def get_item(item_id):
    search = catalog.search(collections=["sentinel-2-l2a"], ids=[item_id])
    items = list(search.items())
    if not items:
        raise RuntimeError('no item '+item_id)
    return pc.sign(items[0])

def sample_ndvi(item, lat, lon, half_px=2):
    # Use asset hrefs for B04 (red) and B08 (nir) - 10m
    b04 = item.assets['B04'].href
    b08 = item.assets['B08'].href
    import rasterio
    from rasterio.windows import Window
    from rasterio.transform import rowcol
    vals = []
    with rasterio.open(b04) as red, rasterio.open(b08) as nir:
        # transform lon,lat to row,col
        r, c = rowcol(red.transform, lon, lat)
        # sample window
        r0 = max(0, r-half_px); c0 = max(0, c-half_px)
        w = Window(c0, r0, half_px*2+1, half_px*2+1)
        red_a = red.read(1, window=w).astype('float32')
        nir_a = nir.read(1, window=w).astype('float32')
        # L2A reflectance scale factor often 10000
        red_a = np.where(red_a==0, np.nan, red_a)
        nir_a = np.where(nir_a==0, np.nan, nir_a)
        ndvi = (nir_a - red_a) / (nir_a + red_a)
        return float(np.nanmean(ndvi)), float(np.nanmedian(ndvi)), int(np.sum(~np.isnan(ndvi)))

results = {}
for label, iid in scenes:
    print('Loading', label, '...')
    try:
        item = get_item(iid)
    except Exception as e:
        print(' fail', e); continue
    results[label] = {}
    for zname, (lat,lon) in zones.items():
        try:
            mean, med, n = sample_ndvi(item, lat, lon)
            results[label][zname] = {'mean': round(mean,3), 'med': round(med,3), 'n': n}
            print(f'  {zname:30s} NDVI={mean:.3f}')
        except Exception as e:
            print(f'  {zname} ERR {e}')
            results[label][zname] = {'error': str(e)}

open('/tmp/ebtl/ndvi_results.json','w').write(json.dumps(results, indent=2))
print('\nSaved /tmp/ebtl/ndvi_results.json')
PY

import json
import numpy as np
import planetary_computer as pc
from pystac_client import Client
import rasterio
from rasterio.windows import Window
from rasterio.transform import rowcol
from rasterio.warp import transform as warp_transform

catalog = Client.open("https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1")

# Zone points refined using Google Maps place + site layout (N wetland / mid campus / S toward reserve)
zones = {
    "N_wetland_percolation": (12.7365, 78.1830),
    "N_panchayat_lake_edge": (12.7355, 78.1815),
    "mid_nursery_food_garden": (12.7345, 78.1825),
    "mid_learning_living": (12.7340, 78.1840),
    "mid_mango_orchard_est": (12.7330, 78.1820),
    "S_restoration_wild": (12.7315, 78.1835),
    "S_far_south_toward_reserve": (12.7300, 78.1840),
    "ref_veppanapilly_forest": (12.7285, 78.1855),
}

scenes = [
    ("2025-12-08_postmono", "S2C_MSIL2A_20251208T051221_R019_T43PHQ_20251208T081319"),
    ("2024-12-08_postmono", "S2B_MSIL2A_20241208T051119_R019_T43PHQ_20241208T075639"),
    ("2024-03-23_dry", "S2B_MSIL2A_20240323T050649_R019_T43PHQ_20240323T101425"),
    ("2025-04-12_dry", "S2C_MSIL2A_20250412T050711_R019_T43PHQ_20250412T102015"),
]

def get_item(item_id):
    items = list(catalog.search(collections=["sentinel-2-l2a"], ids=[item_id]).items())
    return pc.sign(items[0])

def sample_ndvi(item, lat, lon, half_px=4):
    with rasterio.open(item.assets['B04'].href) as red, rasterio.open(item.assets['B08'].href) as nir:
        xs, ys = warp_transform('EPSG:4326', red.crs, [lon], [lat])
        r, c = rowcol(red.transform, xs[0], ys[0])
        r0 = max(0, r-half_px); c0 = max(0, c-half_px)
        w = Window(c0, r0, half_px*2+1, half_px*2+1)
        red_a = red.read(1, window=w).astype('float32')
        nir_a = nir.read(1, window=w).astype('float32')
        # Sentinel-2 L2A Processing Baseline >=4.0: offset -1000, quant 10000
        # Detect if values look like with offset (typical soil ~1500-2500)
        # Apply offset correction if median > 1000 (post PB04)
        if np.nanmedian(red_a) > 1000:
            red_a = (red_a - 1000.0) / 10000.0
            nir_a = (nir_a - 1000.0) / 10000.0
        else:
            red_a = red_a / 10000.0
            nir_a = nir_a / 10000.0
        # clip negatives from offset
        red_a = np.clip(red_a, 0, None)
        nir_a = np.clip(nir_a, 0, None)
        ndvi = (nir_a - red_a) / (nir_a + red_a + 1e-6)
        return float(np.nanmean(ndvi)), float(np.nanmedian(ndvi)), int(ndvi.size)

results = {}
for label, iid in scenes:
    print('Loading', label, '...')
    item = get_item(iid)
    results[label] = {}
    for zname, (lat,lon) in zones.items():
        mean, med, n = sample_ndvi(item, lat, lon)
        results[label][zname] = {'mean': round(mean,3), 'med': round(med,3), 'n': n}
        print(f'  {zname:30s} NDVI={mean:.3f}')

open('/tmp/ebtl/ndvi_results.json','w').write(json.dumps({'zones':zones,'results':results}, indent=2))

print('\n=== RANK dry 2025-04-12 (lowest first = struggling) ===')
for z,v in sorted(results['2025-04-12_dry'].items(), key=lambda x: x[1]['mean']):
    print(f"  {v['mean']:.3f}  {z}")
print('\n=== RANK postmono 2025-12-08 (highest first = greener) ===')
for z,v in sorted(results['2025-12-08_postmono'].items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]['mean']):
    print(f"  {v['mean']:.3f}  {z}")
print('\n=== YoY dry change 2024-03 -> 2025-04 ===')
for z in zones:
    a=results['2024-03-23_dry'][z]['mean']; b=results['2025-04-12_dry'][z]['mean']
    print(f"  {b-a:+.3f}  {z}  ({a:.3f}->{b:.3f})")
print('\n=== Seasonal recovery dry2025 -> postmono2025 ===')
for z in zones:
    a=results['2025-04-12_dry'][z]['mean']; b=results['2025-12-08_postmono'][z]['mean']
    print(f"  {b-a:+.3f}  {z}  ({a:.3f}->{b:.3f})")

content.text:
**Verdict:** The nursery and northern waterworks are the strongest parts of EBTL; the **southern parcels**, **mango orchards (especially wetland-sited ones)**, and **drought-stressed 2023 plantings** are the main places to inspect next.

---

### Field priority map (inspect in this order)

| Rank | Place (site map labels) | Status | Why inspect next |
|------|-------------------------|--------|------------------|
| **1** | **Southern restoration & wild zones** (toward Veppanapilly RF) | Under-attended until mid-2024; now the stated push | July 2024 newsletter: south “has received little attention till now”; plan was cluster planting + leave regeneration gaps |
| **2** | **Mango orchard blocks (~20 acres)** — especially trees in **potential wetlands** | Struggling / mismatche | Remove failing mangoes; check native interplants; wetlands are wrong microhabitat for mango |
| **3** | **Already-treated “green circle” plots** (earthworks + 2023 plantings near catchments) | Recovering after failed monsoon | ~6,000+ natives planted; needed emergency irrigation; start survival M&E here first |
| **4** | **Northern wetland, percolation ponds, northernmost pond + swales** | Doing relatively well | Core water system; check siltation, bund/swale damage, wildlife water rings after monsoon |
| **5** | **Wild-zone irrigation lines / forest edge** | Damage + conflict pressure | May 2024 elephant crushed pipes; deer/boar at ponds; HEC risk nearby |
| **6** | **Vegetable / food-garden beds** | Paused under drought | Left idle to spare water for nursery; check wildlife browse and whether beds need rebuild |
| **7** | **Native nursery** | Best-performing | 110 spp / ~15k capacity; sapling giveaways — routine check only |

**Doing best (monitor, don’t divert scarce labour):** nursery; northern water catchments/ponds; planted plots that put out new shoots after June 2024 rains.  
**Struggling / high risk:** southern untreated land (management gap); wetland mangoes; drought-hit plantings without a survival census; elephant-damaged infrastructure on the wild edge.

---

### Method (so you can check it)

**Sources**
1. Official zone map: [ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/) (`/static/images/ebtl-map-new.png`) — wetland, percolation ponds, Panchayat lake, nursery/food garden, learning/living, restoration & wild zones, Veppanapilly RF.
2. Newsletters (Google Drive folder linked from the site): [June 2023](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1t1_X4f1PjG2YhZtM8Qio8E8cmaKkNLk-/view), [Oct 2023](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PcpKa3bYnJxw0s78qdwWhn_WDAW-IvqE/view), [Feb/Mar 2024](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1f1R1rHA_rjCHDDqB4nHTtrXVWC-Le2CF/view), [July 2024](https://drive.google.com/file/d/122I9j4fVdXYpfqMCGb2n4gNFTtRsXEwb/view).
3. Location: Plus Code **P5MM+H9**, Budhimutlu (~12.7339°N, 78.1834°E).
4. Sentinel-2 L2A NDVI (Microsoft Planetary Computer), ~90×90 m windows around zone centroids, PB≥4 offset applied.

**Key ground facts used**
- Green circles on the July 2024 map = waterworks + invasive clearing + planting already done.
- South flagged as next work area (July 2024).
- 2023 NE monsoon largely failed → hills brown, saplings irrigated from open well; veg beds paused; farm wildlife raids up.
- Mango monoculture on ~20 acres; some in wetlands; remove struggling trees + interplant natives.
- Nursery healthy enough to donate saplings.

**Satellite cross-check (NDVI mean)**

| Zone sample | Dry 2024-03-23 | Dry 2025-04-12 | Post-mono 2025-12-08 |
|-------------|----------------|----------------|----------------------|
| N wetland / percolation | 0.23 | 0.37 | 0.66 |
| N lake edge | 0.22 | 0.30 | 0.65 |
| Mid nursery / food garden | 0.24 | 0.44 | 0.66 |
| Mid mango (est.) | 0.30 | 0.45 | 0.66 |
| Mid learning/living | 0.32 | 0.45 | 0.40 |
| S restoration/wild | 0.34 | 0.57 | 0.77 |
| S far south / reserve edge | 0.33 | 0.56 | 0.78 |
| Ref: Veppanapilly forest | 0.31 | 0.51 | 0.77 |

**How to read this with the newsletters:** South is greenest (forest-edge / reserve influence), so high NDVI ≠ “job done”—it still ranks **#1 for inspection** because management attention lagged. North is driest in the dry season but recovers strongly after rain (wetland phenology + waterworks). Mid campus built area stays low NDVI by design. Year-on-year dry NDVI rose across zones after the bad 2023 monsoon (+0.08 to +0.23).

**Caveats:** Zone points are approximate centroids from the public map + Maps pin, not surveyed plot polygons. NDVI does not separate planted natives from mango, weeds, or forest spillover. No public plot-level survival rates yet (M&E was only starting as of July 2024).The first satellite NDVI job hung and was stopped; a cleaner re-run finished successfully and those numbers are already in the priority map above. No change to the inspection ranking.
